title: Edge proxy buffering impact on KV-cache streaming throughput and tail latency
content:
Purpose:
Quick field investigation into how edge/ingress proxy buffering settings interact with inference-side KV-cache stalls and token-streaming workloads. Goal is pragmatic config guidance we can ship to customers and a reproducible microbenchmark to catch regressions.

Background/context: notes to self
- Streaming responses (small chunks, frequent flushes) are common for low-latency token generation.
- Redis/KV-cache misses or slow disk-backed cold-starts cause brief server-side stalls between token emissions.
- Proxies (Envoy/NGINX/HAProxy) often buffer or coalesce write syscalls which changes tail behavior and can hide backpressure or amplify head-of-line (HOL) effects.
- There are two tension points: per-stream latency vs overall throughput (connections and memory for many concurrent streams).

Testbed summary (single-machine-ish microbench):
- Client runner: 8 vCPU GCP C2 instance, custom loadgen (node + low-level sockets).
- Server: 16 vCPU + A10 GPU (inference runtime build with KV-cache stub that can inject delay), Linux 5.15, kernels tuned only for baseline.
- Proxies tested: Envoy 1.30 (default), Envoy tuned, NGINX 1.24 (default), NGINX tuned (proxy_buffering off or buffer sizes lowered), HAProxy 2.7 (streaming mode).
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming, HTTP/2 server push-like streaming (gRPC bidi-style and raw HTTP/2 DATA frames), gRPC over HTTP/2 (go-grpc).
- Workload: 50 concurrent sessions, each session issues a single streaming request that emits tokens until finished. Average token payload ~28B (small). Server-side token interval baseline = 2ms; artificial KV miss injected 20% of requests causing a 60–120ms stall between token bursts to simulate slow cache fallback.

Key knobs tested:
- proxy_buffering (nginx): on/off and buffer sizes (proxy_buffer_size, proxy_buffers)
- envoy: max_connection_duration, enable_http2_recv_window_override, stream idle / flush_interval (via ext_proc experiment), upstream_flush_interval
- tcp: TCP_NODELAY on upstream sockets, TCP_CORK toggles (where possible)
- http2: SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE, SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS
- client behavior: connection reuse (1 connection per client vs pooled many clients per connection)

Metrics captured:
- per-token emission latency (server-to-client observed delta), p50/p95/p99
- request completion time (end-to-end)
- throughput (tokens/sec) aggregated
- number of active upstream connections and proxy queue length (where visible)
- proxy memory for buffers (approx via /proc)
- traces: when token was emitted by runtime vs when read by client (to attribute buffering)

Results (aggregate, approximate — this is field notes, numbers are rounded):
1) Baseline direct (client -> server, no proxy), TCP_NODELAY on:
   - p50 token latency: 2.1ms
   - p95 token latency: 8.6ms
   - p99 token latency: 25ms
   - throughput: 37k tokens/s
   Observed behavior: token emission from runtime closely matches client read times; KV miss stalls appear as local pauses only.

2) Envoy default (HTTP/2 multiplexing upstream, default flush/window settings):
   - p50: 2.4ms
   - p95: 12ms
   - p99: 120ms (heavy long-tail spikes)
   - throughput: 35k tokens/s
   Observations: p99 spikes correlate with KV miss events. Envoy appears to coalesce writes (small writes held until internal buffer threshold or flush) which delays first token after a stall by tens to hundreds of ms. Multiplexing slightly amplifies HOL: when one stream stalls, related internal write buffers sometimes delayed flushes for other streams until a flush event.

3) Envoy tuned (set http2_settings.initial_window_size=256k, upstream_http1_max_pending=0, enable upstream flushes via x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms to small value, tcp_nodelay upstream):
   - p50: 2.3ms
   - p95: 9ms
   - p99: 28ms
   - throughput: 36k tokens/s
   Notes: tuning reduces p99 significantly. The big wins are disabling internal coalescing for streaming routes and ensuring TCP_NODELAY on upstream sockets.

4) NGINX default (proxy_buffering on):
   - p50: 2.6ms
   - p95: 42ms
   - p99: 180ms
   - throughput: 33k tokens/s
   Explanation: nginx buffers small chunks and only flushes on buffer full or request end. Large p95/p99 during KV miss windows.

5) NGINX proxy_buffering off (and proxy_request_buffering off in some configs):
   - p50: 2.2ms
   - p95: 10ms
   - p99: 30ms
   - throughput: 36k tokens/s
   Comment: turning buffering off approximates direct path. Memory usage increases (per-connection) because nginx must pass through data immediately.

6) gRPC bidi (go-grpc default flow control) behind envoy default:
   - p95/p99 worse than raw HTTP/2 in default envoy due to extra flow-control windows and coarse flush behavior in gRPC stacks. Tuning initial window and keepalive reduces this.

7) HAProxy (streaming mode) with tcp-nodelay: behaved close to direct path; p99s lower than Envoy default but still higher than direct if backend stalls were common.

Top-level takeaways / rules of thumb:
- Proxies that buffer to optimize throughput (NGINX default, Envoy without streaming tuning) can massively inflate tail latency for token-by-token streaming workloads when the server experiences transient stalls (KV misses).
- For streaming routes we should default to pass-through behaviour: disable buffering, enable TCP_NODELAY on upstreams, and tune HTTP/2 initial window so the first few DATA frames aren't stuck behind flow control.
- Multiplexing (HTTP/2) can improve connection utilization but can introduce HOL effects at proxy-level buffers; ensure per-stream flushing semantics (or prefer 1 stream per connection for ultra-low tail) when tail latency matters.
- gRPC stacks need separate attention because language client libs and proxies both apply flow-control and buffering. Always include gRPC-specific flow-control knobs in the checklist.

Operational guidance (minimal safe config for streaming endpoints):
- Envoy: for streaming route(s): set upstream tcp_nodelay true, increase http2 initial window (e.g. 128k–256k), set per-stream flush interval to small (1–5ms) via custom filter if available, track envoy drain/flush metrics.
- NGINX: for streaming locations: proxy_buffering off; disable proxy_request_buffering; set tcp_nodelay on upstream; keep proxy_buffers small to avoid coalescing.
- HAProxy: enable streaming mode and TCP_NODELAY on both sides.
- App/runtime: when emitting small tokens, ensure you call flush at the framework boundary (writable.flush) so proxies see a write and don't coalesce at application layer.

Instrumenting to detect proxy-induced tails:
- Capture server emit timestamps and client receive timestamps and compute delta (trace id per request). If server->client delta > expected by >50ms at p99, mark as proxy buffering candidate.
- Export proxy queue length / buffer occupancy metrics where available (envoy: upstream_cx_active, http_mixer stats, custom admin stats); add an alert rule for sudden correlated p99 spikes and buffer growth.

Open questions / follow-ups (todo):
- Re-run with realistic multi-tenant ingress (many services behind one Envoy) to validate HOL across services not just streams.
- Test effect of kernel-level coalescing: TCP_CORK toggles on server soldered path (hard to flip in higher-level runtimes).
- Measure memory cost per-connection when proxy buffering is disabled at scale (simulate 10k concurrent streaming clients).
- Add a microbenchmark harness in repo: ./bench/proxy-streaming that can replay this workload and produce golden p99 numbers for PR gating.

Action items:
- (Maya) draft a recommended proxy config snippet for streaming routes and post to #serving-runtime by EOD 2026-02-19.
- (Liam) prototype envoy filter to force per-data-frame flush or small flush intervals; measure CPU overhead.
- (Priya) produce a scaled mem footprint sim for nginx with buffering disabled.

References and links (tickets, PRs, slack):
- ENG-2148 (follow-up to streaming proxy incidents)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/782 (bench harness sketch)
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime (ts 1645123456.789) with sample traces attached.

Notes to self: keep these field figures as heuristics. When we push to configs for Hosted, add canary with detailed trace sampling (capture sample of server-emit vs client-receive) to confirm we didn't regress throughput for other non-streaming endpoints.

End of notes.
